passages.happening: ‘For the day is near, the Day of the LORD is near. It will be a day of clouds, a time of doom for the nations’ (verse 3). A sword will come on Egypt, and anguish on Cush (verse 4). ‘The allies of Egypt will fall, and her proud strength will collapse’ (verse 6). God will put an end to Egypt's hordes by the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, the most ruthless of nations (verses 10-11). He will dry up the Nile's channels, destroy the idols of Memphis, and bring judgment on Egypt's cities from north to south (verses 12-19).
passages.hearers:
The Day of the LORD was the prophets' phrase for the time when God acts decisively in judgment. Earlier prophets turned it against Israel itself; here Ezekiel turns it against Egypt. It does not always mean the end of the world; it means the day when God's rule breaks into history.

The cities cover Egypt from north to south. Memphis, called Noph, was the ancient capital near modern Cairo. Zoan, called Tanis, and Pi-beseth, Bubastis, lay in the eastern Delta. On was Heliopolis, the center of the sun cult. Cush lay to the south, in what is now Sudan.
passages.later: Zephaniah called the day of the LORD ‘a day of clouds and blackness’ (Zephaniah 1:15). Jeremiah also spoke against Egypt and its cities (Jeremiah 46:13-14).
passages.asks: Egypt's proud strength was the first thing to collapse. Ask where your strength has made you proud. And ask what it would mean to trust in God's strength instead.

passages.happening: In the eleventh year God says, ‘Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt. See, it has not been bound up for healing, or splinted for strength to hold the sword’ (verse 21). He will break both of Pharaoh's arms, the strong one and the broken one, and scatter the Egyptians (verses 22-23). ‘I will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king and place My sword in his hand’ (verse 24), and Pharaoh will groan before him like a mortally wounded man. Then they will know that he is the LORD (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
This word is dated to the spring of 587 BC, a few months after 29:1. The broken arm is almost certainly the failure of Pharaoh Hophra's army, which marched toward Jerusalem during the siege and then withdrew when the Babylonians moved against it. According to the Greek historian Herodotus, Hophra was later overthrown by one of his own officers, Amasis, around 570 BC.

The arm was a royal symbol of power in Egypt; kings were shown with a raised arm striking down enemies. Israel remembered that the LORD had brought them out of Egypt with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Now God breaks Pharaoh's arm and puts his own sword in Babylon's hand.
passages.later: The LORD brought Israel out of Egypt ‘with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm’ (Deuteronomy 5:15). Jeremiah told Zedekiah that Pharaoh's army would go home (Jeremiah 37:7).
passages.asks: The arm Judah hoped would save it was already broken. Ask where you are still hoping in something that has already failed you. And ask what it would mean to let it go.
